extracted.intended_audience: students and researchers learning graduate-level probability and stochastic processes (Brownian motion)
extracted.subtask_description: Definitions, constructions, and foundational properties of one- and multi-dimensional Brownian motion, including continuity, scaling, Markov and strong Markov properties, 0–1 laws, stopping-time facts, and path regularity results. Suited to readers proving theorems or constructing Brownian motion rigorously.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of one-dimensional Brownian motion
rubrics_metrics.description: A real-valued process Bt, t ≥ 0, satisfying (a) independent increments: for t0 < t1 < ... < tn the increments B(t0), B(t1)-B(t0), ..., B(tn)-B(tn−1) are independent; (b) Gaussian increments with law P(B(s+t)-B(s) ∈ A) = ∫_A (2πt)^{-1/2} exp(−x^2/2t) dx (i.e., increments are N(0,t)); (c) with probability one the sample paths t → Bt are continuous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These three items together are the canonical defining properties; (a) gives independent increments, (b) specifies the normal law with variance t, and (c) enforces path continuity. The text emphasizes intuition (CLT) and immediate consequences like translation invariance and scaling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equivalent Gaussian-covariance definition
rubrics_metrics.description: Bt, t ≥ 0 is Brownian motion starting at 0 iff (a0) Bt is a Gaussian process, (b0) E Bs = 0 and E Bs Bt = s ∧ t, and (c0) paths are a.s. continuous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This formulation specifies all finite-dimensional distributions via mean zero and covariance s∧t and is shown equivalent to the increment/normal-definition. Use this when exploiting Gaussian process structure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Translation invariance
rubrics_metrics.description: {Bt − B0, t ≥ 0} is independent of B0 and has the same distribution as a Brownian motion with B0 = 0.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follows from independence of increments; proved via π-λ theorem. Useful when reducing to the B0 = 0 case in proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Brownian scaling relation
rubrics_metrics.description: If B0 = 0 then for any t > 0, {B_{s t}, s ≥ 0} d= {t^{1/2} B_s, s ≥ 0}; finite-dimensional distributions agree after scaling time by t and space by t^{1/2}.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used throughout (e.g., to reduce general times to unit time) and to derive path regularity and limit results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Construction from consistent finite-dimensional distributions (Kolmogorov extension)
rubrics_metrics.description: Define finite-dimensional measures µ_{x,t1,...,tn} via transition densities p_t(a,b) = (2πt)^{-1/2} exp(−(b−a)^2/2t); consistency of these f.d.d.'s yields a probability on path space Ω_o, then use dyadic rationals and Kolmogorov continuity to obtain a measure concentrated on continuous paths.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Highlights the two-step construction: (i) Kolmogorov extension on countable time sets (dyadics), (ii) Kolmogorov continuity theorem to extend to continuous paths and transfer measure to (C, C).

rubrics_metrics.name: Kolmogorov continuity criterion (Theorem 7.1.3)
rubrics_metrics.description: If E|X_s − X_t|^β ≤ K|t−s|^{1+α} for α, β > 0, then for γ < α/β with probability one there is C(ω) s.t. |X(q) − X(r)| ≤ C|q−r|^γ for all q,r in dyadic rationals in [0,1].
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provides a quantitative condition to obtain (Hölder) regularity of sample paths; used to show uniform continuity on dyadics and to extend to continuous-time paths. The proof uses Chebyshev and Borel–Cantelli plus a dyadic decomposition lemma.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hölder regularity of Brownian paths (Wiener)
rubrics_metrics.description: Brownian paths are Hölder continuous of any exponent γ < 1/2 (Theorem 7.1.5).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combines moments E|B_t − B_s|^{2m} = C_m |t−s|^m with Kolmogorov's criterion and letting m→∞. Useful when estimating moduli of continuity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-differentiability / not Lipschitz at any point
rubrics_metrics.description: With probability one, Brownian paths are not Lipschitz continuous (hence not differentiable) at any point (Theorem 7.1.6); more refined results: not Hölder of exponent >1/2 at any point, and other precise local regularity statements in exercises/remarks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proofs use increment comparisons and scaling; shows almost-sure roughness of paths and justifies stochastic calculus techniques.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multidimensional Brownian motion construction and transition density
rubrics_metrics.description: d-dimensional Brownian motion is given by independent 1-D Brownian coordinates; transition density p_t(x,y) = (2πt)^{-d/2} exp(−|y−x|^2/2t).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Coordinates independent; finite-dimensional distributions factorize; realization as measures P_x on (C, C) with continuous Rd-valued paths.

rubrics_metrics.name: Translation of Markov property to conditional expectation (Theorem 7.2.1)
rubrics_metrics.description: For s ≥ 0 and bounded C-measurable Y, Ex(Y ∘ θ_s | F^+_s) = E_{B_s} Y (i.e., conditional on the sigma-field up to s, the future behaves like a Brownian motion started at B_s).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Statement and proof use monotone class theorem, densities, and the shift θ_s. This is the (strong) Markov property in conditional expectation form for deterministic times (right-continuous filtration).

rubrics_metrics.name: Equality of right-continuous and raw filtrations for conditional expectations
rubrics_metrics.description: If Z ∈ C is bounded then Ex(Z | F^+_s) = Ex(Z | F^o_s) for all s ≥ 0 and x ∈ R^d (Theorem 7.2.2).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shows completions/right-continuous versions and raw sigma-fields agree for bounded continuous functionals; used to deduce Blumenthal's 0–1 law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Blumenthal's 0–1 law (Theorem 7.2.3)
rubrics_metrics.description: The germ σ-field F^+_0 is trivial: if A ∈ F^+_0 then for all x ∈ R^d, P_x(A) ∈ {0,1}.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consequence of previous conditional expectation equality: events determined by arbitrarily small times after 0 have probability 0 or 1; used for local path behavior near 0.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tail σ-field triviality (Theorem 7.2.7)
rubrics_metrics.description: If A belongs to the tail σ-field T = ∩_{t≥0} σ(B_s: s ≥ t) then either P_x(A) ≡ 0 or P_x(A) ≡ 1 for all x.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stronger than Blumenthal's law: events depending only on the distant future have trivial probabilities (0 or 1) for all starting points. Proof uses time-inversion and the Markov property.

rubrics_metrics.name: Immediate hitting from 0 (consequences of 0–1 law)
rubrics_metrics.description: Starting at 0, τ = inf{t ≥ 0 : B_t > 0} equals 0 a.s. and likewise T_0 = inf{t > 0 : B_t = 0} = 0 a.s.; Brownian motion hits both sides and returns to 0 immediately (Theorems 7.2.4 and 7.2.5).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Uses symmetry and Blumenthal's 0–1 law; shows path oscillation at arbitrarily small times.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recurrence and extreme growth (limsup/liminf) results
rubrics_metrics.description: One-dimensional Brownian motion is recurrent: for any starting x, it returns to 0 infinitely often (Theorem 7.2.9). Also lim sup_{t→∞} B_t / √t = ∞ and lim inf = −∞ (Theorem 7.2.8).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Uses tail σ-field triviality and scaling; these are global path-behavior consequences used in long-time analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and basic closure properties of stopping times
rubrics_metrics.description: A random variable S ∈ [0,∞] is a stopping time if {S < t} ∈ F_t for all t (equivalently {S ≤ t} ∈ F_t for right-continuous filtrations). Hitting times of open or closed sets are stopping times; stopping times are closed under monotone limits, min, max, sum, etc. (Theorems 7.3.1–7.3.4 and exercises).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provides the measurable framework for optional sampling and strong Markov statements; proofs use countability (rationals) and right-continuity of the filtration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Information at a stopping time FS and measurability of B_S (Theorem 7.3.8)
rubrics_metrics.description: FS = {A : A ∩ {S ≤ t} ∈ F_t for all t ≥ 0}; the value B_S is measurable with respect to FS (i.e., B_S ∈ FS).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: FS captures the sigma-field of events known at random time S and is the correct conditioning object for the strong Markov property.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strong Markov property at stopping times (Theorem 7.3.9)
rubrics_metrics.description: If (s,ω) → Y_s(ω) is bounded and measurable and S is a stopping time, then for all x ∈ R^d: E_x( Y_S ∘ θ_S | F_S ) = E_{B_S} Y_S on {S < ∞}. Equivalently, conditional on FS, the post-S process behaves like a Brownian motion started at B_S.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Requires Feller property (continuity of x ↦ E_x f(B_t) for bounded continuous f). Proof built from discrete approximations of S (dyadic stopping times), the ordinary Markov property, and monotone class arguments. Fundamental for optional stopping and path decomposition arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Construction of approximating stopping times and right-limit arguments
rubrics_metrics.description: Given a stopping time S define S_n = ([2^n S] + 1)/2^n (first dyadic time > S); S_n are stopping times with S_n ↓ S. These approximations are used in proofs of the strong Markov property and measurability claims (Theorem 7.3.5).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Standard technical device: approximate arbitrary stopping times by simple dyadic-valued stopping times to pass limits in conditional expectations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quadratic variation along nested partitions (exercise remark)
rubrics_metrics.description: For dyadic partitions Π_n the sum over partition increments ∑ Δ_{m,n}^2 converges a.s. to t as mesh→0 (exercise), but the true quadratic variation defined as the supremum over all partitions is ∞.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrates pathwise behavior used in stochastic calculus (martingales and Itô formula section follows later); the distinction between limit over refining specific partitions and supremum over all partitions is emphasized.
